claim: Ustilago maydis causes smut disease in maize with characteristic tumor formation and anthocyanin induction.
source: The biotrophic fungus Ustilago maydis causes smut disease in maize with characteristic tumor formation and anthocyanin induction.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of U. maydis infection.

claim: Anthocyanin biosynthesis is induced by the virulence promoting secreted effector protein Tin2.
source: Here, we show that anthocyanin biosynthesis is induced by the virulence promoting secreted effector protein Tin2.
evidence: This is the main finding presented in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tin2 protein functions inside plant cells.
source: Tin2 protein functions inside plant cells where it interacts with maize protein kinase ZmTTK1.
evidence: Supported by transient expression experiments and microscopy data showing Tin2 function in plant cytosol.

claim: Tin2 interacts with maize protein kinase ZmTTK1.
source: Tin2 protein functions inside plant cells where it interacts with maize protein kinase ZmTTK1.
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Tin2 masks a ubiquitin–proteasome degradation motif in ZmTTK1.
source: Tin2 masks a ubiquitin–proteasome degradation motif in ZmTTK1, thus stabilizing the active kinase.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing ZmTTK1 stabilization in presence of Tin2 and degradation in its absence.

claim: Tin2 stabilizes the active ZmTTK1 kinase.
source: Tin2 masks a ubiquitin–proteasome degradation motif in ZmTTK1, thus stabilizing the active kinase.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot and kinase activity assays showing full-length active ZmTTK1 only in presence of Tin2.

claim: Active ZmTTK1 controls activation of genes in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway.
source: Active ZmTTK1 controls activation of genes in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing upregulation of anthocyanin pathway genes and transient expression experiments.

claim: Enhanced lignin biosynthesis is observed in infected tissue without Tin2.
source: Without Tin2, enhanced lignin biosynthesis is observed in infected tissue and vascular bundles show strong lignification.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing upregulation of lignin biosynthesis genes and microscopy showing lignified vascular bundles.

claim: Vascular bundles show strong lignification in the absence of Tin2.
source: Without Tin2, enhanced lignin biosynthesis is observed in infected tissue and vascular bundles show strong lignification.
evidence: Demonstrated by Safranin O staining of cross-sections showing lignified vascular bundle cells.

claim: Enhanced lignification presumably limits access of fungal hyphae to nutrients needed for massive proliferation.
source: This is presumably limiting access of fungal hyphae to nutrients needed for massive proliferation.
evidence: This is presented as an interpretation of the observed lignification and reduced fungal proliferation.

claim: Maize brown midrib mutants affected in lignin biosynthesis are hypersensitive to U. maydis infection.
source: Consistent with this assertion, we observe that maize brown midrib mutants affected in lignin biosynthesis are hypersensitive to U. maydis infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays showing enhanced disease symptoms in bm mutants.

claim: Tin2 rewires metabolites into the anthocyanin pathway to lower their availability for other defense responses.
source: We speculate that Tin2 rewires metabolites into the anthocyanin pathway to lower their availability for other defense responses.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation based on the observed metabolic changes.

claim: U. maydis is a biotrophic fungus that needs living plant tissue for completion of its sexual cycle and spore formation.
source: U. maydis is a biotrophic fungus that needs living plant tissue for completion of its sexual cycle and spore formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about U. maydis biology.

claim: After penetrating epidermal cells, U. maydis establishes an extended interaction zone in which hyphae are encased by the host plasma membrane.
source: After penetrating epidermal cells and establishing an extended interaction zone in which hyphae are encased by the host plasma membrane, fungal hyphae traverse mesophyll tissue (Doehlemann et al., 2008, 2009), and accumulate in and around vascular bundles (Doehlemann et al., 2008) presumably to obtain nutrients from veins.
evidence: Supported by cited references describing U. maydis infection process.

claim: Fungal hyphae traverse mesophyll tissue during infection.
source: After penetrating epidermal cells and establishing an extended interaction zone in which hyphae are encased by the host plasma membrane, fungal hyphae traverse mesophyll tissue (Doehlemann et al., 2008, 2009), and accumulate in and around vascular bundles (Doehlemann et al., 2008) presumably to obtain nutrients from veins.
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Fungal hyphae accumulate in and around vascular bundles presumably to obtain nutrients from veins.
source: After penetrating epidermal cells and establishing an extended interaction zone in which hyphae are encased by the host plasma membrane, fungal hyphae traverse mesophyll tissue (Doehlemann et al., 2008, 2009), and accumulate in and around vascular bundles (Doehlemann et al., 2008) presumably to obtain nutrients from veins.
evidence: The accumulation is supported by citation, the nutrient acquisition is presented as speculation.

claim: U. maydis secretes hundreds of effector proteins to suppress plant defense responses and reprogram plant signaling and metabolism.
source: During infection, U. maydis secretes hundreds of effector proteins to suppress plant defense responses, and to reprogram plant signaling and metabolism (Doehlemann et al., 2008; Mueller et al., 2008; Horst et al., 2010; Djamei and Kahmann, 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The function of the vast majority of U. maydis effectors is unknown.
source: However, the function of the vast majority of these novel effectors is unknown (Djamei et al., 2011; Djamei and Kahmann, 2012; Hemetsberger et al., 2012; van der Linde et al., 2012; Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Large plant tumors develop at later stages of host colonization that provide the environment for massive fungal proliferation.
source: At later stages of host colonization, large plant tumors develop that provide the environment for massive fungal proliferation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about U. maydis infection.

claim: A high affinity fungal sucrose H+ symporter, Srt1, is upregulated during biotrophic growth and plays a crucial role for fungal nutrition.
source: During biotrophic growth, a high affinity fungal sucrose H+ symporter, Srt1, is upregulated and plays a crucial role for fungal nutrition (Wahl et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Visible changes in host metabolism include an accumulation of anthocyanin in infected areas.
source: Visible changes in host metabolism include an accumulation of anthocyanin in infected areas (Banuett and Herskowitz, 1996; Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Anthocyanin induction was thought to result from unspecific biotic stress caused by microbial infection.
source: Up to date, anthocyanin induction was thought to result from unspecific biotic stress caused by microbial infection (Steyn et al., 2002), and flavonoid-pathway related compounds like luteolinidin have been shown to function as phytoalexins negatively affecting fungal growth (Snyder and Nicholson, 1990; Zuther et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references describing previous understanding.

claim: Flavonoid-pathway related compounds like luteolinidin function as phytoalexins negatively affecting fungal growth.
source: Up to date, anthocyanin induction was thought to result from unspecific biotic stress caused by microbial infection (Steyn et al., 2002), and flavonoid-pathway related compounds like luteolinidin have been shown to function as phytoalexins negatively affecting fungal growth (Snyder and Nicholson, 1990; Zuther et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: No positive link has been established between anthocyanin induction and microbial virulence prior to this study.
source: So far, no positive link has been established between anthocyanin induction and microbial virulence.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: The secreted U. maydis effector Tin2 (Um05302) is specifically responsible for anthocyanin induction in infected seedling tissue.
source: We have recently shown that the secreted U. maydis effector Tin2 (Um05302) is specifically responsible for anthocyanin induction in infected seedling tissue (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The tin2 effector gene resides in the largest effector gene cluster 19A comprising 24 effectors.
source: The tin2 effector gene resides in the largest effector gene cluster 19A comprising 24 effectors (Kämper et al., 2006; Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Deletion of the entire cluster 19A largely abolishes tumor formation and anthocyanin induction.
source: Deletion of the entire cluster 19A largely abolishes tumor formation and anthocyanin induction, although the mutant is still able to grow and complete its life cycle inside the plant tissue (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The cluster 19A deletion mutant is still able to grow and complete its life cycle inside the plant tissue.
source: Deletion of the entire cluster 19A largely abolishes tumor formation and anthocyanin induction, although the mutant is still able to grow and complete its life cycle inside the plant tissue (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Tin2 was previously shown to be responsible for anthocyanin induction during biotrophic growth.
source: Tin2 was previously shown to be responsible for anthocyanin induction during biotrophic growth and was shown to have a weak contribution to virulence (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Tin2 has a weak contribution to virulence.
source: Tin2 was previously shown to be responsible for anthocyanin induction during biotrophic growth and was shown to have a weak contribution to virulence (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Supported by cited reference and confirmed by data in this study.

claim: Introduction of tin2 into SG200Δ19A-1 enhanced tumor formation significantly.
source: Introduction of tin2 enhanced tumor formation significantly and fully restored anthocyanin biosynthesis (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Introduction of tin2 into SG200Δ19A-1 fully restored anthocyanin biosynthesis.
source: Introduction of tin2 enhanced tumor formation significantly and fully restored anthocyanin biosynthesis (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by anthocyanin quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: tin2 is induced during biotrophic growth.
source: In addition, we could demonstrate that tin2 was induced during biotrophic growth (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A SG200Δtin2 mutant colonizes plants efficiently but is attenuated during late proliferation.
source: Microscopic analysis and fungal biomass determination revealed that a SG200Δtin2 mutant did colonize plants efficiently, but was attenuated during late proliferation (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy and fungal biomass quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: Among the top five genes most highly induced after SG200 infection compared to SG200Δtin2, two were related to anthocyanin biosynthesis.
source: Among the top five genes most highly induced after SG200 infection (compared to SG200Δtin2), two were related to anthocyanin biosynthesis (Figure 3—source data 1) and one of these was the second most highly induced gene when SG200-infected tissue was compared with mock inoculated tissue (Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Based on microarray data analysis.

claim: All five genes comprising the anthocyanin pathway were significantly induced in SG200-infected tissue compared to SG200Δtin2-infected tissue.
source: This analysis revealed that all five genes tested were significantly induced in SG200-infected tissue, illustrating that the anthocyanin pathway is transcriptionally induced when U. maydis provides the tin2 effector.
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The anthocyanin pathway is transcriptionally induced when U. maydis provides the tin2 effector.
source: This analysis revealed that all five genes tested were significantly induced in SG200-infected tissue, illustrating that the anthocyanin pathway is transcriptionally induced when U. maydis provides the tin2 effector.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR data.

claim: DIMBOA biosynthesis pathway genes are differentially regulated in response to tin2.
source: Another pathway comprising three differentially regulated genes concerned the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite 2,4-dihydroxy-7-methoxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one (DIMBOA, Figure 3—source data 1; Figure 3D) implicated in aphid and fungal resistance (Ahmad et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on microarray and qPCR data.

claim: DIMBOA is implicated in aphid and fungal resistance.
source: Another pathway comprising three differentially regulated genes concerned the biosynthesis of the secondary metabolite 2,4-dihydroxy-7-methoxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one (DIMBOA, Figure 3—source data 1; Figure 3D) implicated in aphid and fungal resistance (Ahmad et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Bx1, Bx2, Bx5 and Bx8 genes show significant differences in expression between SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected tissue.
source: When the expression levels of eight genes comprising the entire DIMBOA biosynthesis pathway were analyzed by qPCR, we detected significant differences in expression for Bx1, Bx2, Bx5 and Bx8 (Figure 3E) in SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected tissue while we could not detect differences in expression for Bx3, Bx4, Bx6 and Bx7 (not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is an approximately 15-fold increase of anthocyanins in leaf material upon infection with the wild-type strain compared to SG200Δtin2-infected leaves.
source: This revealed an approximately 15-fold increase of anthocyanins in leaf material upon infection with the wild-type strain that was absent in the SG200Δtin2-infected leaves (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by photometric quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The three highly abundant anthocyanins in infected maize leaves are cyanidin 3-glucoside, cyanidin 3-(6''-malonylglucoside), and cyanidin 3-(3'',6''-dimalonylglucoside).
source: By UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis the identity of the three highly abundant anthocyanins in infected maize leaves were determined: cyanidin 3-glucoside (449.0996 Da, C21H21O11+); cyanidin 3-(6''-malonylglucoside) (535.1088 Da, C24H23O14+); cyanidin 3-(3'',6''-dimalonylglucoside) (621.1092 Da, C27H25O17+) and confirmed by MS2 fragmentation studies (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Determined by UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis and MS2 fragmentation.

claim: These cyanidin derivatives were previously described to be the major anthocyanins in maize leaves.
source: These cyanidin derivatives were previously described to be the major anthocyanins in maize leaves (Fossen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Flavonoids are reduced in tissue infected with the tin2 mutant relative to the wild type.
source: In the UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis, we also identified flavonoids and DIBOA-glucoside to be reduced in tissue infected with the tin2 mutant relative to the corresponding wild type (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DIBOA-glucoside is reduced in tissue infected with the tin2 mutant relative to the wild type.
source: In the UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis, we also identified flavonoids and DIBOA-glucoside to be reduced in tissue infected with the tin2 mutant relative to the corresponding wild type (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The three flavonoids identified are orientin 2''-O-rhamnoside, isoorientin 2''-O-rhamnoside, and quercetin-glucoside-rhamnoside.
source: Exact mass as well as MS2 spectra information allowed to identify the three flavonoids as: orientin 2''-O-rhamnoside (594.1585 Da, C27H30O15); isoorientin 2''-O-rhamnoside (594.1585 Da, C27H30O15); quercetin-glucoside-rhamnoside (610.1534, C27H30O16) (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Identified by exact mass and MS2 spectra.

claim: The biosynthesis of these flavonoids branches off the anthocyanin pathway and is likely a side effect of the upregulation of this pathway after infection by wild-type U. maydis.
source: The biosynthesis of these flavonoids branches off the anthocyanin pathway and is likely a side effect of the upregulation of this pathway after infection by wild-type U. maydis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on pathway knowledge and observed expression patterns.

claim: DIBOA-glucoside is regulated by Tin2.
source: In case of DIMBOA biosynthesis we identified 2,4-dihydroxy-1,4-benzoxazin-3-one glucoside (DIBOA-glucoside, 343.0903 Da, C14H17NO9, Figure 4E) to be regulated by Tin2.
evidence: Demonstrated by UPLC-PDA-TOF-MS analysis.

claim: Besides the influence of Tin2 on anthocyanin, additional pathways may be affected directly or indirectly by tin2.
source: These findings suggest that, besides the influence of Tin2 on anthocyanin, additional pathways may be affected directly or indirectly by tin2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observed effects on multiple pathways.

claim: The Tin2 protein does not reveal any conserved InterPro domains.
source: The Tin2 protein does not reveal any conserved InterPro domains.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Orthologous Tin2 proteins are absent in other organisms examined to date but exist in the related smut fungi Sporisorium reilianum and U. scitaminea.
source: Orthologous proteins are absent in other organisms examined to date but exist in the related smut fungi Sporisorium reilianum and U. scitaminea.
evidence: Based on sequence database searches.

claim: The C-terminal third of Tin2 protein shows significant sequence conservation among orthologs.
source: An amino acid alignment revealed significant sequence conservation in the C-terminal third of the protein, whereas the N-terminus showed less conservation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by amino acid alignment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The C-terminal region of Tin2 contains two proline repeat sequences (PxxP).
source: The C-terminal region contains two proline repeat sequences (PxxP), suggesting that this domain might be important for the interaction with other proteins (Saksela et al., 1995; Kay et al., 2000; Dornan et al., 2003) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Observed in sequence analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The proline repeat sequences in Tin2 might be important for interaction with other proteins.
source: The C-terminal region contains two proline repeat sequences (PxxP), suggesting that this domain might be important for the interaction with other proteins (Saksela et al., 1995; Kay et al., 2000; Dornan et al., 2003) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is speculation based on known functions of proline-rich motifs cited in the literature.

claim: Tin21-206 truncated by one amino acid complemented as efficiently as full-length Tin21-207.
source: Tin21-206 truncated by one amino acid complemented as efficiently as full-length Tin21-207 (Figure 1A,B), whereas Tin21-202 lacking five amino acid residues at the C-terminus could neither complement for tumor formation nor anthocyanin induction (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Tin21-202 lacking five amino acid residues at the C-terminus could neither complement for tumor formation nor anthocyanin induction.
source: Tin21-206 truncated by one amino acid complemented as efficiently as full-length Tin21-207 (Figure 1A,B), whereas Tin21-202 lacking five amino acid residues at the C-terminus could neither complement for tumor formation nor anthocyanin induction (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Tin2AAAAA protein, in which the five most C-terminal amino acids were substituted by alanine, was largely unable to complement.
source: Tin2AAAAA protein, in which the five most C-terminal amino acids were substituted by alanine, was also largely unable to complement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C-terminal region of Tin2 is crucial for tumor formation as well as anthocyanin induction.
source: These results indicated that the C-terminal region of Tin2 is crucial for tumor formation as well as anthocyanin induction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the truncation experiments.

claim: Full-length Tin2-HA was detectable in the culture supernatant.
source: To demonstrate that the Tin2 protein can be secreted, we constructed a strain constitutively expressing a biologically active Tin2-HA fusion protein (Figure 5A,B) and showed that full-length Tin2-HA was detectable in the culture supernatant (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 5C.

claim: mCherry fluorescence of Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 could be observed around fungal hyphae after infection.
source: After infection, mCherry fluorescence could be observed around fungal hyphae (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The fluorescence of Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 resided in the apoplast when subjected to plasmolysis.
source: When subjected to plasmolysis, which enlarges the apoplastic compartment, the fluorescence of Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 resided in the apoplast (Figure 6B), demonstrating secretion (Doehlemann et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy after plasmolysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Strain SG200Δtin2-Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 elicited anthocyanin induction, but compared to SG200 the appearance was delayed.
source: Strain SG200Δtin2-Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 elicited anthocyanin induction, but compared to SG200 the appearance was delayed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 fusion protein is only partially functional.
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 fusion protein is only partially functional.
source: Strain SG200Δtin2-Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 elicited anthocyanin induction, but compared to SG200 the appearance was delayed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the Tin21-25-mCherry-Tin226-207 fusion protein is only partially functional.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the delayed anthocyanin induction.

claim: mCherry-Tin226-207 was never detected in the cytosol of infected plants.
source: In addition, mCherry-Tin226-207 was never detected in the cytosol of infected plants.
evidence: This is a negative observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Anthocyanin biosynthesis is occurring in the cytosol of plant cells.
source: Since anthocyanin biosynthesis is occurring in the cytosol of plant cells (Holton and Cornish, 1995), we expected that Tin2 would translocate to plant cells after being secreted.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Expression of tin2 without its secretion signal under the CaMV 35S promoter in maize leaf epidermal cells did not induce anthocyanin in uninfected leaves.
source: To demonstrate a function of Tin2 in the plant cytosol, we expressed tin2 without its secretion signal under the CaMV 35S promoter in maize leaf epidermal cells after biolistic bombardment. As this did not induce anthocyanin (Figure 6C, leftmost panel), we repeated the experiment with leaves from plants infected with SG200Δtin2.
evidence: Demonstrated by transient expression experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Tin226-207 induced anthocyanin in SG200Δtin2-infected leaves when expressed transiently.
source: Here, anthocyanin could be induced by Tin226-207 (Figure 6C, third panel), was absent in infected leaves without tin2 expression (Figure 6C, second panel) and could also not be observed when biologically inactive Tin226-202 was expressed (Figure 6C, rightmost panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by transient expression experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Anthocyanin production was observed in the bombarded cell that also expressed cytosolic mCherry when p35S-Tin226-207 and p35S-mCherry were co-introduced.
source: To confirm that anthocyanin is produced in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue transiently transformed with tin2, p35S-Tin226-207 and p35S-mCherry as transformation control were introduced simultaneously in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue. Anthocyanin production, detected by its dark color in bright field microscopy, was observed in the bombarded cell that also expressed cytosolic mCherry (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cells neighboring the transformed cell also accumulated anthocyanin.
source: Interestingly, cells neighboring the transformed cell also accumulated anthocyanin (Figure 6D, red arrow).
evidence: Observed in confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6D.

claim: mCherry-Tin226-207 was found to spread into non-transformed neighboring cells when transiently expressed in uninfected maize leaves.
source: When biolistic transformation of uninfected maize leaves was carried out with a plasmid expressing mCherry-Tin226-207, the fusion protein was found to spread into non-transformed neighboring cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Symplastic spreading was observed for the Cmu1 effector of U. maydis and for several translocated effectors of Magnaporthe oryzae.
source: Symplastic spreading was observed for the Cmu1 effector of U. maydis and for several translocated effectors of Magnaporthe oryzae (Khang et al., 2010; Djamei et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Tin2 functions within the plant cytosol.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that Tin2 functions within the plant cytosol and suggest that Tin2 may prepare maize cells for the infection by U. maydis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transient expression experiments.

claim: Tin2 may prepare maize cells for the infection by U. maydis.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that Tin2 functions within the plant cytosol and suggest that Tin2 may prepare maize cells for the infection by U. maydis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed cell-to-cell spreading.

claim: Full-length ZmTTK1 was able to interact with Tin226-207 and Tin226-206 in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: In yeast two-hybrid assays, full-length ZmTTK1 was able to interact with Tin226-207 and Tin226-206, while no interaction was observed with Tin226-202 lacking biological activity (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No interaction was observed between ZmTTK1 and Tin226-202 lacking biological activity in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: In yeast two-hybrid assays, full-length ZmTTK1 was able to interact with Tin226-207 and Tin226-206, while no interaction was observed with Tin226-202 lacking biological activity (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Physical interaction between recombinant Strep-ZmTTK1 protein and recombinant GST-Tin226-207 protein was demonstrated by co-IP.
source: Physical interaction between recombinant Strep-ZmTTK1 protein and recombinant GST-Tin226-207 protein was demonstrated by co-IP using GST-Tin226-202 as negative control (Figure 9A).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Recombinant ZmTTK1 purified from E. coli was expressed as full-length protein.
source: Recombinant ZmTTK1 purified from E. coli was expressed as full-length protein (Figure 9B) and showed in vitro kinase activity determined with MBP (myelin basic protein) as substrate.
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Recombinant ZmTTK1 showed in vitro kinase activity determined with MBP as substrate.
source: Recombinant ZmTTK1 purified from E. coli was expressed as full-length protein (Figure 9B) and showed in vitro kinase activity determined with MBP (myelin basic protein) as substrate.
evidence: Demonstrated by kinase assay shown in Figure 9C.

claim: No significant differences in MBP phosphorylation were apparent in the presence or absence of Tin2 in vitro.
source: However, no significant differences in MBP phosphorylation were apparent in the presence or absence of Tin2 (Figure 9C).
evidence: Demonstrated by kinase assay shown in Figure 9C.

claim: ZmTTK1 protein proved highly unstable when transiently expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana.
source: To examine whether Tin2 protein affects ZmTTK1 activity in vivo, we transiently expressed ZmTTK1 protein in Nicotiana benthamiana. In this system, ZmTTK1 protein proved highly unstable and the N-terminal region could not be detected (Figure 10A).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The N-terminal region of ZmTTK1 contains a phosphodegron-like motif DSGxS.
source: This region contains a phosphodegron-like motif DSGxS, which, when phosphorylated at serine residues, serves as a recognition motif for the ubiquitin ligase complex leading to protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Ravid and Hochstrasser, 2008; Spoel et al., 2009).
evidence: Identified by sequence analysis and supported by cited references.

claim: Phosphorylated DSGxS motif serves as a recognition motif for the ubiquitin ligase complex leading to protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: This region contains a phosphodegron-like motif DSGxS, which, when phosphorylated at serine residues, serves as a recognition motif for the ubiquitin ligase complex leading to protein degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Ravid and Hochstrasser, 2008; Spoel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Addition of proteasome inhibitor MG132 to N. benthamiana cells transiently expressing ZmTTK1-HA allowed detection of full-length protein.
source: Addition of proteasome inhibitor MG132 to N. benthamiana cells transiently expressing ZmTTK1-HA allowed detection of full-length protein (Figure 10B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 10B.

claim: ZmTTK1S279/282A-HA protein carrying alanine substitutions at positions serine 279 and serine 282 in the phosphodegron-like motif could be expressed as full-length protein in the transient N. benthamiana system.
source: In addition, ZmTTK1S279/282A-HA protein carrying alanine substitutions at positions serine 279 and serine 282 in the phosphodegron-like motif could be expressed as full-length protein in the transient N. benthamiana system (Figure 10B).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Poly-ubiquitinated ZmTTK1-HA protein accumulated in ZmTTK1-HA expressing plant cells treated with MG132.
source: Furthermore, poly-ubiquitinated ZmTTK1-HA protein accumulated in ZmTTK1-HA expressing plant cells treated with MG132 but not in ZmTTK1S279/282A-HA expressing N. benthamiana cells (Figure 10C).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot after immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The phosphodegron-like motif in ZmTTK1 promotes partial degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: These results indicate that the phosphodegron-like motif in ZmTTK1 promotes partial degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MG132 and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The region in ZmTTK1 that interacts with Tin2 coincides with the variable region containing the phosphodegron-motif.
source: The region in ZmTTK1 that interacts with Tin2 was mapped by yeast two-hybrid assays and shown to coincide with the variable region containing the phosphodegron-motif (Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid mapping shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Full-length ZmTTK1 was detected when ZmTTK1-HA was co-expressed in N. benthamiana together with functional Tin226-207.
source: Next, when ZmTTK1-HA was co-expressed in N. benthamiana together with functional Tin226-207, we detected full-length ZmTTK1, but not when non-functional truncated Tin226-202 was co-expressed with ZmTTK1 (Figure 10D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by western blot shown in Figure 10D,E.

claim: Immunoprecipitated ZmTTK1-HA co-expressed with Tin226-207 showed MBP phosphorylation activity in vitro.
source: Furthermore, immunoprecipitated ZmTTK1-HA co-expressed with Tin226-207 showed MBP phosphorylation activity in vitro while expression of ZmTTK1-HA alone or co-expression of ZmTTK1-HA with truncated Tin226-202 did not yield an immunoprecipitate with phosphorylation activity (Figure 10E, bottom panel).
evidence: Demonstrated by kinase assay shown in Figure 10E.

claim: Tin2 protein targets the phosphodegron-containing region of ZmTTK1, stabilizing full-length, active ZmTTK1.
source: This illustrates that Tin2 protein targets the phosphodegron-containing region of ZmTTK1, stabilizing full-length, active ZmTTK1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-expression and kinase activity experiments.

claim: The number of cells showing a YFP signal was increased significantly when ZmTTK1-YFP and mCherry-Tin226-207 were co-expressed compared to when ZmTTK1-YFP was expressed alone in maize.
source: When ZmTTK1-YFP and mCherry-Tin226-207 were co-expressed, the number of cells showing a YFP signal was increased significantly compared to the situation when ZmTTK1-YFP was expressed alone, and in addition, a significant percentage of cells showed strong YFP fluorescence in the co-expression conditions (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 11A,B.

claim: The ZmTTK1-YFP fusion protein is unstable in maize epidermal cells.
source: This suggests that the ZmTTK1-YFP fusion protein is also unstable in maize epidermal cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the increased signal upon Tin2 co-expression.

claim: Co-expression of Tin2 stabilizes the ZmTTK1-YFP fusion protein in maize.
source: Co-expression of Tin2 stabilizes the fusion protein, similar to what was observed in N. benthamiana.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the increased YFP signal upon co-expression.

claim: Weak anthocyanin induction could be observed when the stabilized form of the kinase, ZmTTK1S279/282A, was transiently co-expressed with cytoplasmic mCherry in leaves infected with SG200Δtin2.
source: To elucidate whether there is a direct link between ZmTTK1 activity and anthocyanin induction, the stabilized form of the kinase, ZmTTK1S279/282A, was transiently co-expressed with cytoplasmic mCherry in leaves infected with SG200Δtin2. In transiently transformed cells weak anthocyanin induction could be observed (Figure 11C).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy shown in Figure 11C.

claim: In maize anthocyanin biosynthesis genes are positively regulated via ZmR1 and ZmC1 transcription factors.
source: In maize anthocyanin biosynthesis genes are positively regulated via ZmR1 and ZmC1 transcription factors (Ludwig and Wessler, 1990; Dooner et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: mCherry-ZmC1 localized to the nucleus, and this localization did not change significantly in the presence of Tin226-207 and ZmTTK1.
source: mCherry-ZmC1 localized to the nucleus, and this localization did not change significantly in the presence of Tin226-207 and ZmTTK1 (Figure 11D).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 11D.

claim: When mCherry-ZmR1 was expressed alone, the fusion protein showed weak cytoplasmic and nuclear localization.
source: When mCherry-ZmR1 was expressed alone, the fusion protein showed weak cytoplasmic and nuclear localization (Figure 11E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 11E.

claim: When co-expressed with Tin226-207 and ZmTTK1, mCherry-ZmR1 protein showed almost exclusively intense nuclear localization.
source: However, when co-expressed with Tin226-207 and ZmTTK1, mCherry-ZmR1 protein showed almost exclusively intense nuclear localization (Figure 11D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal microscopy and quantification shown in Figure 11D,E.

claim: ZmTTK1 protein kinase stabilized by Tin2 might phosphorylate the ZmR1 protein, which is then imported into the nucleus.
source: These results suggest that ZmTTK1 protein kinase stabilized by Tin2 might phosphorylate the ZmR1 protein, which is then imported into the nucleus (or is retained there) and induces anthocyanin biosynthetic genes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed nuclear localization change.

claim: In the general phenylpropanoid pathway, phenylalanine is converted to 4-coumaroyl CoA, which then serves as a precursor for both anthocyanins and lignin.
source: In the general phenylpropanoid pathway, phenylalanine is converted to 4-coumaroyl CoA, which then serves as a precursor for both, anthocyanins and lignin (Figure 12A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the phenylpropanoid pathway.

claim: The phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) gene in the general part of the pathway was significantly upregulated in both SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected tissue compared to mock inoculation.
source: qPCR analysis demonstrated that the phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) gene in the general part of the pathway was significantly upregulated in both SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected tissue compared to mock inoculation (Figure 12B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: One of the two CCR genes of maize (GRMZM2G131836) was clearly induced after U. maydis infection, but there was no difference in induction in SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected leaves.
source: One of the two 'cinnamoyl-CoA reductase' (CCR) genes of maize one was not induced, while the other one (GRMZM2G131836) was clearly induced after U. maydis infection, but there was no difference in induction in SG200- and SG200Δtin2-infected leaves (Figure 12).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The major 4-coumarate-CoA ligase (4CL) gene in the lignin-specific branch (GRMZM2G075333) was not differentially regulated.
source: The major 4-coumarate-CoA ligase (4CL) gene in the lignin-specific branch (GRMZM2G075333; based on homology with sorghum; Saballos et al., 2012) was not differentially regulated, while the flavonoid-related 4CL (GRMZM2G054013) was downregulated in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue compared to SG200-infected tissue (Figure 12B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The flavonoid-related 4CL (GRMZM2G054013) was downregulated in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue compared to SG200-infected tissue.
source: The major 4-coumarate-CoA ligase (4CL) gene in the lignin-specific branch (GRMZM2G075333; based on homology with sorghum; Saballos et al., 2012) was not differentially regulated, while the flavonoid-related 4CL (GRMZM2G054013) was downregulated in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue compared to SG200-infected tissue (Figure 12B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: Of the six cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD) genes, four genes were significantly upregulated in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue.
source: Of the six cinnamyl alcohol dehydrogenase (CAD) genes, four genes were significantly upregulated in SG200Δtin2-infected tissue (Figure 12B).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 12B.

claim: The enhanced expression of several lignin biosynthesis genes after infection with the tin2 mutant coincided with a transcriptional upregulation of several plant cell wall remodeling genes.
source: The enhanced expression of several lignin biosynthesis genes after infection with the tin2 mutant coincided with an transcriptional upregulation of several plant cell wall remodeling genes (Figure 12—source data 1) and a decrease in ferulic acid (Figure 4F), which is involved in crosslinking hemicellulosic polysaccharides and provides a nucleation site for lignification (Grabber et al., 2002), suggesting a connection between these processes.
evidence: Based on microarray data and metabolite analysis.

claim: Ferulic acid is involved in crosslinking hemicellulosic polysaccharides and provides a nucleation site for lignification.
source: The enhanced expression of several lignin biosynthesis genes after infection with the tin2 mutant coincided with an transcriptional upregulation of several plant cell wall remodeling genes (Figure 12—source data 1) and a decrease in ferulic acid (Figure 4F), which is involved in crosslinking hemicellulosic polysaccharides and provides a nucleation site for lignification (Grabber et al., 2002), suggesting a connection between these processes.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: In a maize chalcone synthase mutant (c2), virulence of U. maydis SG200 was attenuated.
source: Furthermore, in a maize chalcone synthase mutant (c2), in which the biosynthetic pathway to anthocyanins is blocked, and in which there could conceivably be more precursor going into the lignin branch, virulence of U. maydis SG200 was attenuated (Figure 13).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 13.

claim: Quantification of total lignin content from isolated cell walls in wild-type maize revealed a small increase in leaf tissue infected with tin2 mutant strains relative to SG200-infected material that was statistically significant in one of three analyzed mutants.
source: Quantification of total lignin content from isolated cell walls in wild-type maize (cv. Early Golden Bantam) revealed a small increase in leaf tissue infected with tin2 mutant strains relative to SG200-infected material that was statistically significant in one of three analyzed mutants (Figure 14A).
evidence: Demonstrated by lignin quantification shown in Figure 14A.

claim: Except for the bm2 mutant, all other single bm mutants displayed elevated virulence symptoms after U. maydis infection.
source: Except for the bm2 mutant, all other single bm mutants displayed elevated virulence symptoms after U. maydis infection, with bm3 showing the strongest effect (Figure 14C).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 14C.

claim: The bm3 mutant showed the strongest effect in elevated virulence symptoms.
source: Except for the bm2 mutant, all other single bm mutants displayed elevated virulence symptoms after U. maydis infection, with bm3 showing the strongest effect (Figure 14C).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 14C.

claim: The bm3-bm4 double mutant showed dramatically enhanced disease symptoms.
source: Of the double mutants, the bm3-bm4 mutant showed dramatically enhanced disease symptoms, while disease symptoms in the bm2-bm3 double mutant was lower than in the single bm3 mutant (Figure 14C), suggesting a negative effect of the bm2 mutation on virulence in this combination.
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 14C.

claim: Disease symptoms in the bm2-bm3 double mutant was lower than in the single bm3 mutant.
source: Of the double mutants, the bm3-bm4 mutant showed dramatically enhanced disease symptoms, while disease symptoms in the bm2-bm3 double mutant was lower than in the single bm3 mutant (Figure 14C), suggesting a negative effect of the bm2 mutation on virulence in this combination.
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 14C.

claim: The bm2 mutation has a negative effect on virulence in the bm2-bm3 combination.
source: Of the double mutants, the bm3-bm4 mutant showed dramatically enhanced disease symptoms, while disease symptoms in the bm2-bm3 double mutant was lower than in the single bm3 mutant (Figure 14C), suggesting a negative effect of the bm2 mutation on virulence in this combination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed disease symptoms.

claim: When bm2 was combined with bm1, virulence was comparable to the single bm1 mutant.
source: When bm2 was combined with bm1, virulence was comparable to the single bm1 mutant (Figure 14C).
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays shown in Figure 14C.

claim: In the bm mutants (with the exception of the single bm2 mutant) leaf tumors were much more spread and covered the entire leaf area from the injection hole to the stem.
source: After infection with SG200, more than 80% of leaf tumors stayed locally confined, while in the bm mutants (with the exception of the single bm2 mutant) leaf tumors were much more spread and covered the entire leaf area from the injection hole to the stem (Figure 14B,D), suggesting that lignification restricts U. maydis growth and spread in the infected tissue.
evidence: Demonstrated by infection assays and symptom distribution analysis shown in Figure 14B,D.

claim: Lignification restricts U. maydis growth and spread in the infected tissue.
source: After infection with SG200, more than 80% of leaf tumors stayed locally confined, while in the bm mutants (with the exception of the single bm2 mutant) leaf tumors were much more spread and covered the entire leaf area from the injection hole to the stem (Figure 14B,D), suggesting that lignification restricts U. maydis growth and spread in the infected tissue.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed symptom distribution in bm mutants.

claim: Strongly lignified cells were observed in vascular bundle tissue in cross sections of maize leaves infected with SG200Δtin2.
source: In line with this assertion, we observed strongly lignified cells in vascular bundle tissue in cross sections of maize leaves infected with SG200Δtin2 and could only rarely observe fungal hyphae in bundle sheath cells (Figure 14E).
evidence: Demonstrated by Safranin O staining shown in Figure 14E.

claim: Fungal hyphae were only rarely observed in bundle sheath cells in tissue infected with SG200Δtin2.
source: In line with this assertion, we observed strongly lignified cells in vascular bundle tissue in cross sections of maize leaves infected with SG200Δtin2 and could only rarely observe fungal hyphae in bundle sheath cells (Figure 14E).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy shown in Figure 14E.

claim: Lignification was significantly less pronounced in SG200-infected tissue compared to SG200Δtin2-infected tissue.
source: By contrast, lignification was significantly less pronounced in SG200-infected tissue (Figure 14F) and in tissue infected by SG200Δtin3 (Figure 14G), a mutant lacking another effector from cluster 19A that does not affect anthocyanin induction (Brefort et al., in press).
evidence: Demonstrated by Safranin O staining shown in Figure 14F.

claim: SG200 and SG200Δtin3 hyphae were readily detected inside bundle sheath cells.
source: Additionally, SG200 and SG200Δtin3 hyphae were readily detected inside bundle sheath cells (Figure 14F,G).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy shown in Figure 14F,G.

claim: Anthocyanin induction by the Tin2 effector attenuates lignification of vascular bundle cells, conceivably facilitating fungal access to nutrients in vascular bundle tissue.
source: This suggests that anthocyanin induction by the Tin2 effector attenuates lignification of vascular bundle cells, conceivably facilitating fungal access to nutrients in vascular bundle tissue.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed lignification patterns and fungal colonization.

claim: ZmTTK1 is an uncharacterized kinase, with its kinase domain located at the C-terminus.
source: ZmTTK1 is an uncharacterized kinase, with its kinase domain located at the C-terminus (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Maize may contain two putative paralogs of ZmTTK1 (GRMZM2G088409; GRMZM2G068192) with highly conserved kinase domains but reduced homology in the N-terminal domains.
source: Maize may contain two putative paralogs of ZmTTK1 (GRMZM2G088409; GRMZM2G068192) with highly conserved kinase domains (63 and 65% identity), but reduced homology in the N-terminal domains (34% and 36% identity, respectively).
evidence: Based on sequence database searches and alignment.

claim: Orthologs of ZmTTK1 are found in monocot plants like Sorghum bicolor, Oryza sativa, Hordeum vulgare, and Brachypodium distachyon and display high amino acid sequence identity with ZmTTK1 from maize (between 75% and 94%).
source: Orthologs are found in monocot plants like Sorghum bicolor, Oryza sativa, Hordeum vulgare, and Brachypodium distachyon and these display high amino acid sequence identity with ZmTTK1 from maize (between 75% and 94%) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana encodes a putative ortholog of ZmTTK1 (AT2G40120), but the amino acid identity is significantly lower (57%).
source: Arabidopsis thaliana also encodes a putative ortholog of ZmTTK1 (AT2G40120), but in this case the amino acid identity is significantly lower (57%) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: ZmTTK1 orthologs from monocot plants display highly conserved N- and C-terminal domains, which are separated by a more variable central domain.
source: ZmTTK1 orthologs from monocot plants display highly conserved N- and C-terminal domains, which are separated by a more variable central domain (Figure 7A,C).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: In the related A. thaliana protein, the N-terminal region shows only patchy homology to the monocot proteins and the central domain is missing.
source: In the related A. thaliana protein, the N-terminal region shows only patchy homology to the monocot proteins and the central domain is missing (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 7A.

claim: None of the ZmTTK1 orthologs have been functionally characterized to date.
source: None of these proteins have been functionally characterized to date.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge.

claim: The link between Tin2 and anthocyanin biosynthesis appears direct and occurs through the stabilization of the kinase ZmTTK1 via Tin2.
source: The link between Tin2 and anthocyanin biosynthesis appears direct and occurs through the stabilization of the kinase ZmTTK1 via Tin2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: When U. maydis is lacking tin2, more of the common precursor for anthocyanin and lignin, 4-coumaric acid, is likely to be available for lignin biosynthesis resulting in cell wall fortification in vascular tissue.
source: Conversely, when U. maydis is lacking tin2, more of the common precursor for anthocyanin and lignin, 4-coumaric acid, is likely to be available for lignin biosynthesis (Figure 15) resulting in cell wall fortification in vascular tissue.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed metabolic changes and lignification patterns.

claim: The deposition of lignin in the plant cell wall is considered to provide an undegradable physical barrier to infection.
source: The deposition of lignin in the plant cell wall is considered to provide an undegradable physical barrier to infection (Vance et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The observed decrease in ferulic acid in SG200Δtin2-infected leaves compared to SG200-infected tissue is consistent with increased lignification where ferulic acid acts as a nucleation site for lignin polymerization.
source: The observed decrease in ferulic acid in SG200Δtin2-infected leaves compared to SG200-infected tissue is consistent with increased lignification where ferulic acid acts as a nucleation site for lignin polymerization (Grabber et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the metabolite data and cited reference.

claim: Tin2 affected all steps of the anthocyanin pathway.
source: Tin2 affected all steps of the anthocyanin pathway, but did not affect transcription of all genes coding for lignin pathway components.
evidence: Based on qPCR data showing upregulation of all anthocyanin pathway genes.

claim: Tin2 did not affect transcription of all genes coding for lignin pathway components.
source: Tin2 affected all steps of the anthocyanin pathway, but did not affect transcription of all genes coding for lignin pathway components.
evidence: Based on qPCR data showing differential effects on lignin pathway genes.

claim: The increased susceptibility of maize bm mutants to U. maydis provides strong evidence for a role of lignification in disease resistance.
source: However, the increased susceptibility of maize bm mutants to U. maydis and the increased leaf areas displaying disease symptoms, provide strong evidence for a role of lignification in disease resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bm mutant infection data.

claim: A less lignified cell wall will be easier to penetrate by the fungus.
source: A less lignified cell wall will be easier to penetrate by the fungus.
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms underlying increased susceptibility.

claim: The plant may be less effective at producing defense-related lignin that could slow down the migration of the fungus in bm mutants.
source: The plant may also be less effective at producing defense-related lignin that could slow down the migration of the fungus.
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms underlying increased susceptibility.

claim: The bm2 mutant appears to accumulate a fungitoxic (phenolic) compound.
source: This effect may be due to the accumulation of a fungitoxic (phenolic) compound in this mutant, as has been proposed for the sorghum brown midrib12 mutant, which was shown to be less susceptible to colonization by Fusarium spp. (Funnell-Harris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to sorghum mutants cited in the literature.

claim: In N. attenuata lines in which two CAD genes were silenced, compensatory processes for the structural deficiencies were observed when plants were grown in the field, and such plants accumulated various phenylpropanoids.
source: Also in N. attenuata lines in which two CAD genes were silenced, compensatory processes for the structural deficiencies were observed when plants were grown in the field, and in this case such plants accumulated various phenylpropanoids (Kaur et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Direct effects of Tin2 on lignification are the simplest model to explain the reduced virulence of the tin2 mutant strain.
source: Therefore, while we consider direct effects of Tin2 on lignification to be the simplest model to explain the reduced virulence on the tin2 mutant strain (Figure 15), the situation may in reality be much more complex.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: The situation regarding Tin2's effects may in reality be much more complex than direct effects on lignification.
source: Therefore, while we consider direct effects of Tin2 on lignification to be the simplest model to explain the reduced virulence on the tin2 mutant strain (Figure 15), the situation may in reality be much more complex.
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the interpretation.

claim: In the absence of anthocyanin biosynthesis it could be the enhanced lignification that affects fungal spread.
source: For example we cannot formally rule out that in the absence of anthocyanin biosynthesis it is not actually the enhanced lignification that affects fungal spread but an altered composition of the plant cell walls.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claim: The enhanced disease symptoms observed in the bm mutants could be attributed to a lower incorporation of phenolics rather than to the reduction in lignin.
source: Conversely, the enhanced disease symptoms observed in the bm mutants could also be attributed to an lower incorporation of phenolics rather than to the reduction in lignin, that is in wild-type plants cell wall phenolics may negatively affect fungal growth and restrict pathogen spread.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation considered by the authors.

claim: Reduction in lignin content and changes in lignin subunit composition have been shown to improve biomass conversion in a number of species.
source: Reduction in lignin content and changes in lignin subunit composition have been shown to improve biomass conversion in a number of species (Chen and Dixon, 2007; Studer et al., 2011), including maize, with the bm1 and bm3 mutations leading to 50% higher yields of fermentable sugars on a per-gram-biomass-basis (Vermerris et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Modifying lignin composition in maize has the risk of increased susceptibility to U. maydis, and the associated reduction in yield.
source: Based on the experiments described here, it is clear that modifying lignin composition in maize has the risk of increased susceptibility to U. maydis, and the associated reduction in yield.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bm mutant infection data.

claim: In A. thaliana, the silencing of HCT redirected the metabolic flux into flavonoids through chalcone synthase and this resulted in elevated levels of flavonols and anthocyanin.
source: However, precedence for a connection between lignin and anthocyanin biosynthesis comes from A. thaliana, where the silencing of HCT (hydroxycinnamoyl transferase), the first committed enzyme from the lignin pathway, redirected the metabolic flux into flavonoids through chalcone synthase and this resulted in elevated levels of flavonols and anthocyanin (Besseau et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: Transgenic A. thaliana plants expressing the lignin biosynthesis repressing ZmMYB31 transcription factor from maize redirected carbon flux towards the biosynthesis of anthocyanins.
source: In addition, transgenic A. thaliana plants expressing the lignin biosynthesis repressing ZmMYB31 transcription factor from maize redirected carbon flux towards the biosynthesis of anthocyanins (Fornalé et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: A competition between anthocyanin and lignin pathways for their common precursor has been detected in strawberry.
source: Recently, a competition between anthocyanin and lignin pathways for their common precursor has also been detected in strawberry (Ring et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: In strawberry, plant class III peroxidase (FaPRX27), a gene connected with lignin biosynthesis, is linked to a region implied in fruit color decrease.
source: In that system it was demonstrated that plant class III peroxidase (FaPRX27), a gene connected with lignin biosynthesis, is linked to a region implied in fruit color decrease.
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: In strawberry, the downregulation of chalcone synthase led to an induction of FaPRX27 and this diverted the flux from anthocyanins to lignin.
source: In addition, it was demonstrated that the downregulation of chalcone synthase lead to an induction of FaPRX27 and this diverted the flux from anthocyanins to lignin (Ring et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: There appears to be a metabolic connection between anthocyanin and lignin biosynthesis pathways in monocot as well as dicot systems.
source: Thus, there appears to be a metabolic connection between anthocyanin and lignin biosynthesis pathways in monocot as well as dicot systems and U. maydis may be altering this with the help of Tin2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited examples and the current study.

claim: U. maydis may be altering the metabolic connection between anthocyanin and lignin biosynthesis with the help of Tin2.
source: Thus, there appears to be a metabolic connection between anthocyanin and lignin biosynthesis pathways in monocot as well as dicot systems and U. maydis may be altering this with the help of Tin2.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects of Tin2.

claim: In A. thaliana MYB75 acts as a repressor for the lignin-specific branch of the phenylpropanoid pathway presumably through an interaction with TT8.
source: In A. thaliana MYB75, which is related to maize ZmC1, but is not the closest ortholog, acts as a repressor for the lignin-specific branch of the phenylpropanoid pathway presumably through an interaction with TT8, a bHLH protein related to ZmR1 (Bhargava et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: If a repressive complex for lignin biosynthesis exists in maize, the observed Tin2-mediated nuclear localization of ZmR1 might promote the formation of such a complex.
source: If such a scenario also exists in maize, the observed Tin2-mediated nuclear localization of ZmR1 might actually promote the formation of such a repressive complex for lignin biosynthesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to A. thaliana.

claim: An upregulation of Bx1 and elevated amounts of DIMBOA had previously been detected after colonization of maize by U. maydis.
source: An upregulation of Bx1 and elevated amounts of DIMBOA had previously been detected after colonization of maize by U. maydis (Basse, 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: U. maydis is resistant to DIMBOA while several other fungal pathogens of maize are susceptible.
source: In this context, it had also been demonstrated that U. maydis is resistant to DIMBOA (Basse, 2005) while several other fungal pathogens of maize are susceptible (Glenn et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: The induction of DIMBOA might deter infection by other pathogens in U. maydis infected tissue.
source: This could indicate that the induction of DIMBOA might deter infection by other pathogens in U. maydis infected tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the resistance profile of U. maydis.

claim: In a macro-array based expression analysis of phenylpropanoid and related genes in brown midrib mutants, two genes from the DIMBOA pathway, Bx4 and Bx5, were significantly upregulated in the bm3 mutant.
source: However, in a macro-array based expression analysis of phenylpropanoid and related genes in brown midrib mutants, two genes from the DIMBOA pathway, Bx4 and Bx5, were significantly upregulated in the bm3 mutant, that is the mutant with the strongest effect in lignin biosynthesis (Guillaumie et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: The upregulation of DIMBOA after SG200 infection could be the consequence of the locally reduced lignin content in the infected areas.
source: If true, the upregulation of DIMBOA after SG200 infection could also be the consequence of the locally reduced lignin content in the infected areas.
evidence: This is speculation based on the bm3 mutant data.

claim: For its function, the Tin2 protein must translocate into plant cells after being secreted.
source: For its function, the Tin2 protein must translocate into plant cells after being secreted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional data showing Tin2 acts in the plant cytosol.

claim: Large fluorescent tags fused to effectors may prevent uptake in the U. maydis-maize pathosystem.
source: Based on similar results with Cmu1, another transferred effector (Djamei et al., 2011), we speculate that large fluorescent tags fused to the respective effector prevent uptake in this pathosystem.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations with Cmu1 and Tin2.

claim: Cmu1 and Tin2 do not share obvious common motifs that can be recognized in their primary amino acid sequence that could serve as translocation signal.
source: Cmu1 and Tin2 do not share obvious common motifs that can be recognized in their primary amino acid sequence that could serve as translocation signal, and it remains to be determined how they cross the plant plasma membrane.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis.

claim: It may be necessary to pre-infect plants to obtain high levels of phenylalanine or tyrosine for anthocyanin biosynthesis.
source: We consider that it may be necessary to pre-infect plants to obtain high levels of phenylalanine or tyrosine for anthocyanin biosynthesis.
evidence: This is speculation to explain why transient Tin2 expression only induces anthocyanin in pre-infected tissue.

claim: U. maydis infection increases amounts of phenylalanine and tyrosine in infected leaves through Cmu1 and possibly other effectors.
source: These amino acids supply the flavonoid pathway and U. maydis infection was shown to increase their amounts in infected leaves through Cmu1 and possibly other effectors (Doehlemann et al., 2008; Djamei et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: In maize, anthocyanin induction is connected to kernel development.
source: In maize, anthocyanin induction is connected to kernel development (Holton and Cornish, 1995) and is also observed when coleoptiles are exposed to UV-B (Beggs and Wellman, 1985).
evidence: Supported by cited references.

claim: Anthocyanin induction is observed when maize coleoptiles are exposed to UV-B.
source: In maize, anthocyanin induction is connected to kernel development (Holton and Cornish, 1995) and is also observed when coleoptiles are exposed to UV-B (Beggs and Wellman, 1985).
evidence: Supported by cited reference.

claim: There will be a native regulatory system stabilizing the ZmTTK1 protein kinase in conditions where anthocyanin is naturally induced.
source: We hypothesize that there will be a native regulatory system stabilizing the ZmTTK1 protein kinase in such conditions, and Tin2 may mimic this regulator.
evidence: This is speculation about the natural function of ZmTTK1.

claim: Tin2 may mimic a native regulator that stabilizes ZmTTK1.
source: We hypothesize that there will be a native regulatory system stabilizing the ZmTTK1 protein kinase in such conditions, and Tin2 may mimic this regulator.
evidence: This is speculation about Tin2's mechanism of action.

claim: ZmTTK1 orthologs in barley and B. distachyon have substitutions in critical serine residues of the phosphodegron motif DSGxS.
source: Interestingly, ZmTTK1 orthologs in barley and B. distachyon have substitutions in critical serine residues of the phosphodegron motif DSGxS, and in the related kinase from A. thaliana this region is missing altogether (Figure 7A).
